newsitem.title: UK: Labour is sympathetic to petrol reforms - official.
newsitem.headline: Labour is sympathetic to petrol reforms - official.

text.p: A Labour government would be "sympathetic" to implementing reforms aimed at softening the impact of a nationwide petrol price war that shut nearly 10 percent of Britain's filling stations last year, a Labour official said on Thursday.

Labour would also meet with oil companies and retailers and ensure that motorists in rural areas had access to petrol at reasonable prices, Nigel Griffith, spokesman for consumer affairs for the opposition party and a member of Parliament from Edinburgh, told Reuters.
"I think you can say that we are studying the committee's findings with care and I think it's fair to say that Labour is likely to be sympathetic to implementing them," he said.

"We're determined to ensure that consumers get access to petrol in rural areas as well as elsewhere at reasonable prices, and that those aspects of the report which would lead to that would be our top priority," he said.

Asked if British motorists were harmed by the ferocious price war in the petrol market that has kept British pump prices cheap in Europe but closed 1,500 petrol sites last year, Griffith said: "There are causes for concern."

Labour's stance on the downstream oil sector will not be included in its election manifesto on Thursday, he said. Elections are set for May 1 and Labour, ahead in the polls, is poised to take power for the first time since 1979.

British prices are amongst the lowest in Europe but independent retailers believe the campaign, along with stiff competition from the supermarkets, will wipe out many filling stations, particularly outside the cities, and ultimately lead to higher prices.

The Trade and Industry Committee conducted hearings last July about six months after Esso Petroleum, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, launched its Pricewatch campaign promising to match its lowest-priced competitors at the pump.

The committee recalled in December the Minister of Energy, Lord Fraser of Carmyllie, and the Director General of Fair Trading, John Bridgeman, after the government brushed off most of its 11 recommendations.
The following are the recommendations from the committee last year:
* The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) investigate the allegations of discrimination across channels of trade.

* A code of practice be drawn up through negotiation between the OFT and the petrol retail industry, covering the contractual relationships between wholesalers and retailers, including provisions for speedy and binding arbitration of disputes.
* The Director General of Fair Trading (DGFT) to continuously monitor the petrol retailing industry.
* Bring forward measures to reform competition law and increase the powers of the DGFT as a matter of urgency.
* Duty be levied on petrol refined in Britain as it leaves storage rather than as it leaves the refinery.
* Strategic stock requirements passed on to companies in a way that does not distort competition.
* A commitment to publish rack prices and subsidiary company accounts to be the subject of undertakings given by refiners and retailers to the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry.
* All retailers with a significant market share to provide the OFT regularly with statistics showing the level of their retail sales and market share on a regional and national basis.
* Consider ways that taxation levied on petrol could be adjusted to ensure that retailers in rural areas are not disadvantaged.
* The OFT's monitoring to include measures to detect the emergence of local monopolies.

* Endorse the recommendation by the Environment Committee that the government give due consideration to the problems in rural areas, and grant exemptions for small and remote stations from Stage II of the Petrol Recovery Directive if it is implemented.
